passages.title: What drives heavy-duty fuel consumption
passages.source_reference: Synthetic RAG corpus (non-OEM educational text; not manufacturer guidance)
passages.content_excerpt: Fuel consumption of a heavy-duty truck is primarily driven by the power demanded at the wheels, which depends on the vehicle mass, speed, acceleration, aerodynamic drag, rolling resistance and road gradient. Higher demanded power requires more fuel per second. The fuel rate (L/h) is therefore an immediate proxy for engine load and driver demand, not a fixed vehicle property.

passages.title: Aerodynamic drag grows with speed
passages.source_reference: Synthetic RAG corpus (non-OEM educational text; not manufacturer guidance)
passages.content_excerpt: Aerodynamic drag rises with the square of speed, so the fuel cost per kilometre climbs quickly above about 70-80 kph. High-speed cruising consumes disproportionately more fuel than moderate-speed cruising for a heavy truck.

passages.title: Payload and fuel consumption
passages.source_reference: Synthetic RAG corpus (non-OEM educational text; not manufacturer guidance)
passages.content_excerpt: Adding payload increases vehicle mass, which raises rolling resistance and the force needed to accelerate and climb. Heavier loads therefore increase fuel rate, especially during acceleration and on grades. The effect is roughly proportional to mass on flat ground and stronger on gradients.

passages.title: How road grade affects fuel and
passages.source_reference: Synthetic RAG corpus (non-OEM educational text; not manufacturer guidance)
passages.content_excerpt: Climbing a grade requires extra force equal to the component of vehicle weight along the slope, which directly increases engine load and fuel rate. Descending can allow engine braking or coasting with little or no fuel. Steep, sustained uphill sections sharply increase fuel per kilometre.

passages.title: Gross vehicle weight limits
passages.source_reference: Synthetic RAG corpus (non-OEM educational text; not manufacturer guidance)
passages.content_excerpt: A truck's gross vehicle weight (GVW) is a rated maximum. Operating near GVW increases fuel use and drivetrain stress; operating at very low load improves fuel economy but reduces productivity per trip.
